title: Detailed Laboratory Protocols - PhIP-Seq and MIPSA
subtitle: With QC Procedures, Variability Indicators, and Protocol Evolution
---


*Variability key: 🟢 Low | 🟡 Medium | 🔴 High*

*QC notation: ✓ = confirmed in published protocol or Infinity Bio report | ◇ = recommended best practice, not confirmed as routinely applied*

---

# PART 1: PhIP-Seq Protocol

## Background and Evolution

| Version | Reference | Key Changes |
|---|---|---|
| **v1** | Larman et al., *Nat Biotechnol*, 2011 | 36-aa tiles, human proteome, 2-round panning, magnetic bead IP |
| **v2** | Xu et al. (VirScan), *Science*, 2015 | 56-aa tiles, 28-aa overlap, virome library (93,904 peptides) |
| **v3** | Mohan & Larman et al., *Nat Protoc*, 2018 | Standardised protocol, pepsyn tool, single-round panning, Z-score analysis |
| **v4** | Shrock et al., *Bio Protoc*, 2022 | Video supplement, IEDB antigens added, reproducibility emphasis |

The core wet lab steps have remained largely stable since v2. The most consequential protocol change was the switch from two-round to single-round panning (v2 → v3), which improved quantitative linearity but means pre-2018 datasets are not directly comparable to modern data without harmonisation.

---

## Phase A: Library Design and Construction

---

### Step A1 — Proteome Selection and Peptide Tile Design
🟢 **Low variability**

**Description**

- Protein sequences of interest (pathogen proteomes, human proteome, allergens, or custom panels) downloaded in FASTA format
- Tiled into overlapping peptide fragments using the *pepsyn* tool with defined length and overlap parameters
- v1 (2011): 36-aa tiles with 18-aa overlap
- v3+ (2018 onward): 56-aa tiles with 28-aa overlap — longer tiles improve sensitivity for epitopes near tile boundaries
- Each peptide sequence back-translated to a DNA sequence optimised for T7 phage expression
- Flanking cloning sequences appended to each oligo

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Sequence verification of in silico library against source proteome (completeness check) — described in Mohan & Larman 2018
- ✓ Confirm even tiling — no gaps in protein sequence coverage — confirmed standard practice
- ◇ Check for duplicate or near-identical tiles that could confound alignment
- ◇ GC content distribution of designed oligos (extreme GC reduces synthesis yield)
- ◇ Reference database version documented and locked

**Variability Introduced**

- Library design is entirely computational — variability minimal when reference proteomes are versioned and pepsyn parameters are fixed
- Main risk: reference database version drift across studies creates non-comparable libraries between labs or time points
- Tile length and overlap choice is a systematic design decision, not a source of run-to-run variability

---

### Step A2 — Oligonucleotide Synthesis
🔴 **High variability**

**Description**

- Designed DNA sequences synthesised as a pooled oligonucleotide library on microarray-based platforms (e.g. Agilent, Twist Bioscience)
- Each oligo encodes one peptide tile plus flanking primer sequences
- Libraries range from 50,000 to >700,000 distinct sequences per synthesis run
- Synthesised pool eluted and amplified by PCR to generate sufficient material for cloning

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ NGS of amplified oligo pool to verify library complexity and representation evenness — described in Mohan & Larman 2018
- ✓ Gel electrophoresis to confirm oligo length distribution — confirmed standard practice
- ◇ Target: each library member within 10-fold of median (in practice >100-fold range is common — this is a known limitation, not a failure criterion)
- ◇ Flag severely underrepresented sequences before proceeding to cloning

**Variability Introduced**

- Microarray synthesis introduces systematic representation bias — some sequences synthesised at lower yield due to GC content, secondary structure, and positional effects on the array
- Persistent source of library imbalance that downstream normalisation must address
- One of the most consequential sources of background non-uniformity in the final count matrix
- Batch-to-batch variation between synthesis runs is real and not fully correctable

---

### Step A3 — Cloning into T7 Phage Display Vector
🔴 **High variability**

**Description**

- Amplified oligo pool cloned into T7 bacteriophage display vector (T7Select system, Novagen/Millipore)
- T7 preferred over M13: displays larger inserts (up to 1,000 aa), smaller particle (~60 nm), no membrane export requirement — allows peptides with internal cysteines
- Insert fused to T7 10B capsid protein — peptide displayed on phage surface, linking genotype to phenotype
- Recombinant phage packaged in vitro and used to infect E. coli BLT5403 for amplification

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Plaque titration to determine phage library titre (target: >10⁸ pfu/ml) — confirmed in Mohan & Larman 2018
- ✓ PCR of individual plaques to verify insert presence — confirmed standard practice
- ◇ Deep sequencing of packaged library to confirm complexity maintained through cloning
- ◇ Calculate fraction of phage carrying insert vs empty vector

**Variability Introduced**

- Cloning efficiency is not uniform — sequences encoding toxic or poorly expressed peptides are selectively lost
- Compounds synthesis bias from A2: library complexity after cloning is reliably lower than designed complexity
- Losses at this step are irreversible — dropped library members cannot be recovered

---

## Phase B: Library Propagation

---

### Step B1 — E. coli Infection and Phage Amplification
🟡 **Medium variability**

**Description**

- Packaged phage library used to infect E. coli BLT5403 (contains T7 RNA polymerase under IPTG-inducible control)
- Infected culture grown to lysis; lysate cleared by centrifugation
- Amplified phage stock generated for use in all downstream immunoprecipitation experiments
- Multiplicity of infection (MOI) — the phage:bacteria ratio — must be controlled to ensure uniform amplification

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Phage titre of amplified stock (pfu/ml) — confirmed standard practice
- ◇ Deep sequencing of amplified stock to verify library complexity maintained vs pre-amplification
- ◇ Confirm no catastrophic dropout of specific library members
- ◇ Monitor lysis time (too fast or too slow indicates culture problems)

**Variability Introduced**

- Phage encoding peptides that confer growth disadvantage to E. coli will be underrepresented after amplification
- Library representation can shift between amplification rounds — particularly for aged or re-amplified stocks
- Standardising MOI and growth conditions reduces but does not eliminate representation drift

---

## Phase C: Immunoprecipitation (Panning)

---

### Step C1 — Serum Pre-adsorption
🟡 **Medium variability**

**Description**

- Serum pre-adsorbed against E. coli lysate and/or empty phage particles (no insert) to remove non-specific antibodies
- Performed by incubation at 4°C followed by magnetic bead capture and removal
- Reduces background binding to E. coli antigens and phage coat proteins
- Not standardised until v3 (Mohan & Larman 2018)

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Monitor serum volume and dilution factor — confirmed in 2018 protocol
- ◇ Confirm reduction in background binding to empty phage controls post-adsorption
- ◇ Pre-adsorption material must be from the same lot across a study batch

**Variability Introduced**

- Pre-adsorption efficiency varies with serum composition, incubation time, and quality of the blocking material
- Insufficient pre-adsorption inflates background and increases false positive rate
- Excessive pre-adsorption can remove low-affinity true positives

---

### Step C2 — Phage-Antibody Incubation
🔴 **High variability**

**Description**

- Pre-adsorbed serum diluted 1:1000 in PBS-T and incubated with the phage library at 4°C with rotation for 16–18 hours
- Serum antibodies bind to cognate peptide epitopes displayed on the phage surface
- Library used at ~10⁵ phage per library member to ensure adequate representation
- v3 (2018): input IgG concentration normalised across samples to reduce between-sample variability

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Confirm consistent phage input across all samples (measured by titre) — confirmed in 2018 protocol
- ✓ Confirm consistent serum dilution — confirmed standard practice
- ✓ Positive control sera with known reactivity included — confirmed in 2018 protocol
- ✓ Negative controls (PBS or pre-immune serum) — confirmed in 2018 protocol
- ◇ IgG quantification and normalisation of input samples

**Variability Introduced**

- Largest source of sample-to-sample variability in the assay
- Total IgG concentration varies substantially between individuals — affects competition for library members
- Temperature fluctuations and rotation speed inconsistencies affect binding kinetics
- 16–18 hour window introduces time-of-day variability if plates are not processed simultaneously

---

### Step C3 — Immunoprecipitation with Protein A/G Magnetic Beads
🔴 **High variability**

**Description**

- Protein A/G magnetic beads added to capture IgG–phage complexes from the incubation mixture
- Beads separated by magnet and washed 3–5× with PBS-T to remove unbound phage
- Bound phage retained on beads contain the peptides recognised by the individual's antibodies
- v1 (2011): two panning rounds; v3 (2018): single-round panning became standard — two rounds over-enriched non-specific phage and reduced quantitative linearity

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Mock IP control (PBS, no serum) run in parallel — confirmed in 2018 protocol; primary background reference for all data analysis
- ✓ Positive control recovery confirmed — confirmed standard practice
- ◇ Phage titre in wash fractions to confirm adequate washing
- ◇ Bead volume and wash stringency logged and kept consistent across samples

**Variability Introduced**

- Bead capture efficiency varies with bead lot, total IgG load, and wash conditions
- Non-specific sticking of phage to beads is a persistent source of background
- Switch from 2-round to single-round panning (v2 → v3) significantly reduced non-specific enrichment — historical and modern datasets are not directly comparable without harmonisation

---

## Phase D: Sequencing Library Preparation and NGS

---

### Step D1 — PCR Amplification of Phage Inserts
🟡 **Medium variability**

**Description**

- Phage eluted from beads by boiling after final wash
- Insert DNA amplified by PCR using universal primers flanking the cloning site
- Illumina sequencing adapters and sample-specific index barcodes added in same or subsequent indexing PCR
- PCR cycles minimised (typically 20–25) to avoid over-amplification artefacts

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Gel electrophoresis to confirm PCR product at expected size — confirmed standard practice
- ✓ Library quantification by Qubit or qPCR — confirmed in 2018 protocol
- ◇ Check for primer dimer contamination
- ◇ Confirm index diversity across multiplexed samples
- ◇ Minimum input phage threshold before PCR to avoid jackpot effects

**Variability Introduced**

- PCR amplification biases toward shorter or higher-GC inserts
- Jackpot effects (clonal amplification of rare phage) can occur if input phage count is very low
- Consistent input phage numbers across samples partially controls this

---

### Step D2 — Next-Generation Sequencing
🟢 **Low variability**

**Description**

- Multiplexed libraries from all samples pooled and sequenced on Illumina (HiSeq or NextSeq)
- Target: 1–3 million reads per sample
- Single-end 50-bp reads standard — inserts are short enough that paired-end adds little information
- Reads demultiplexed by sample index after sequencing run

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Per-sample read count (target: >500,000 aligned reads; low counts trigger repeat) — confirmed in 2018 protocol
- ✓ Sequencing quality scores (Q30 threshold) — standard Illumina QC
- ◇ Duplication rate per sample
- ◇ Fraction of reads aligning to designed library (unaligned reads indicate contamination or artefacts)

**Variability Introduced**

- NGS is the most reproducible step in the entire protocol
- Run-to-run variability is low given standardised platform and chemistry
- Main technical risk: uneven pooling of samples before sequencing run leads to one sample dominating reads

---

## Phase E: Data Analysis

---

### Step E1 — Read Alignment and Count Matrix Generation
🟢 **Low variability**

**Description**

- Raw reads trimmed and aligned to the designed peptide library using Bowtie2
- Count matrix generated: rows = peptide tiles, columns = samples, values = read counts
- Tiles with zero counts across all samples flagged for investigation
- Phippery pipeline commonly used for integrated processing (alignment, QC, normalisation)

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Alignment rate (target: >85% of reads map to library) — confirmed in Phippery documentation
- ✓ Per-sample read depth and count distribution — confirmed standard practice
- ◇ Pearson correlation between technical replicates (target: ≥0.95)
- ◇ PCA of all samples — controls should cluster separately from patient samples

**Variability Introduced**

- Alignment is a deterministic computational step — minimal variability for fixed aligner parameters
- Parameter choices (mismatch tolerance, multi-mapping handling) affect the count matrix but are fixed within a study

---

### Step E2 — Normalisation and Hit Calling
🟡 **Medium variability**

**Description**

- Read counts normalised using RPM or edgeR TMM normalisation
- Each sample compared against the full set of mock IP controls using one of three methods:
  - **edgeR** (negative binomial GLM): FDR-adjusted p-value < 0.05
  - **BEER** (Bayesian hierarchical model): posterior probability of enrichment; higher sensitivity for weak reactivities
  - **Z-score**: Z = (RPM_sample − mean RPM_mock) / SD RPM_mock; threshold typically Z > 3.5
- All three methods operate at the per-tile level — no formal probe-aggregation across overlapping tiles

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Distribution of fold-over-background values (approximately log-normal with heavy right tail) — confirmed standard practice
- ✓ Positive control enrichment confirmed — confirmed standard practice
- ◇ Mock IPs cluster separately from serum samples in PCA
- ◇ Comparison of hit lists across methods as sensitivity check

**Variability Introduced**

- Choice of statistical method (edgeR vs BEER vs Z-score) affects hit lists — systematic variability, not random
- Particularly consequential for weak or early-stage antibody responses
- No probe-aggregation across overlapping tiles performed in any current pipeline — tile independence assumption is unverified and likely incorrect
- FDR-based thresholds carry all limitations of p-value-derived inference at scale

---

# PART 2: MIPSA Protocol

## Background and Evolution

| Version | Reference | Key Changes |
|---|---|---|
| **v1** | Larman lab, *bioRxiv*, March 2021 | Proof-of-concept; IFNL3 autoantibody; ~50% cis-barcoding; release factors excluded |
| **v2** | Credle & Larman et al., *Nat Biomed Eng*, 2022 | 11,076-ORF library; Gateway cloning; pDEST-MIPSA vector; I-SceI linearisation; 10× UCI/ORF |
| **v3** | Infinity Bio, ongoing (VirSIGHT / HuSIGHT) | Peptide tile libraries; Dolphyn-optimised selection; 96-well plate format; column 12 controls |

---

## Phase A: Vector Construction and Library Assembly

---

### Step A1 — pDEST-MIPSA Vector Design
🟢 **Low variability**

**Description**

- MIPSA Gateway Destination vector (pDEST-MIPSA) encodes in order: T7 promoter → UCI barcode → E. coli RBS → N-terminal HaloTag (891 nt) → FLAG epitope → Gateway recombination sites → I-SceI site
- UCI barcode sequence: (SW)₁₈–AGGGA–(SW)₁₈ where S = C/G and W = A/T — isothermal design ensures balanced GC content
- Each ORF inserted by Gateway LR recombination from an entry clone library (e.g. human ORFeome)
- Each ORF represented by ~10 UCIs (unique barcoded copies) — designed redundancy enabling probe-aggregation analysis

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Sanger sequencing of recombined clones to verify ORF orientation and reading frame fusion to HaloTag — confirmed in Credle & Larman 2022
- ◇ Deep sequencing of plasmid pool to verify UCI barcode diversity (~10 UCIs per ORF)
- ◇ Confirm no frameshifts or stop codons introduced at recombination junctions

**Variability Introduced**

- Vector design is fixed — minimal variability at this step
- Gateway recombination efficiency varies by ORF size but is well-established
- UCI diversity is stochastic by design — the isothermal sequence ensures uniqueness and identifiability
- ~10× UCI redundancy per ORF is the key design feature enabling multi-probe statistical aggregation

---

### Step A2 — Plasmid Linearisation
🟢 **Low variability**

**Description**

- Circular pDEST-MIPSA plasmid pool linearised at the I-SceI restriction site downstream of each ORF
- Prevents read-through transcription beyond the ORF
- Uncontrolled transcript length would interfere with RT-priming geometry and HaloTag cis-coupling in Phase B
- Linearised DNA purified by column or ethanol precipitation

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Gel electrophoresis to confirm complete linearisation (no supercoiled band remaining) — confirmed in Credle & Larman 2022
- ◇ DNA quantification post-purification (Qubit or NanoDrop)

**Variability Introduced**

- I-SceI is a highly efficient and specific homing endonuclease — low intrinsic variability
- Incomplete linearisation is the primary failure mode and is readily detected by gel electrophoresis
- Operator error (wrong buffer, wrong temperature) is the main risk

---

## Phase B: Self-Assembly — IVT, Reverse Transcription, and Cell-Free Translation

> ⚠ Steps B1–B3 are tightly coupled. The RNA produced in B1 serves simultaneously as the translation template and the molecule to which the cDNA barcode attaches in B2, before self-assembly occurs during translation in B3.

---

### Step B1 — In Vitro Transcription (IVT)
🟡 **Medium variability**

**Description**

- Linearised pDEST-MIPSA pool used as template for in vitro transcription using T7 RNA polymerase
- Produces pool of RNA molecules, each containing: UCI barcode + HaloTag coding sequence + ORF sequence
- RNA serves a dual role: translation template AND the molecule to which the UCI cDNA barcode is attached in B2
- RNA purified and stored at −80°C in small aliquots to prevent freeze-thaw degradation

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ RNA yield and concentration (Qubit) — confirmed standard practice
- ◇ RNA integrity check (Bioanalyzer or TapeStation) — degraded RNA reduces translation efficiency
- ◇ Confirm expected size distribution of transcripts across ORF sizes
- ◇ RNase contamination check — strict RNase-free technique required throughout

**Variability Introduced**

- RNA is inherently less stable than DNA — the most chemically fragile intermediate in the pipeline
- Transcription efficiency varies by template GC content and secondary structure
- RNase contamination is a critical risk — a single contaminated reagent can destroy the entire pool
- RNA degradation between IVT and the coupled RT/translation step is a meaningful source of per-ORF efficiency variability

---

### Step B2 — Reverse Transcription with HaloLigand-Conjugated Primer
🔴 **High variability**

**Description**

- RT primer conjugated to a succinimidyl ester–haloalkane (HaloLigand) moiety annealed to each RNA at position −32 nt upstream of the AUG start codon
- Position −32 empirically determined: primers within 20 nt of the RBS interfere with ribosome assembly and abolish translation; −32 is closest position that does not reduce translation yield
- Reverse transcriptase synthesises cDNA from the UCI barcode region, producing an RNA:cDNA hybrid
- HaloLigand-conjugated cDNA is now physically proximal to the ribosome entry site, poised for cis coupling during translation in B3

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ◇ Confirm RT primer incorporation by gel or bioanalyzer
- ◇ RT efficiency assessed by qPCR on cDNA product
- ◇ Confirm HaloLigand coupling chemistry is intact (supplier QC certificates; functional validation by test translation with FLAG western blot)
- ◇ Primer batch QC — each new lot should be validated before library-scale use

**Variability Introduced**

- Most technically demanding and variable step in the MIPSA protocol
- RT efficiency varies with RNA secondary structure, template GC content, and primer batch quality
- HaloLigand conjugation chemistry must be intact — degraded or improperly conjugated primer breaks the barcode–protein link entirely
- Batch-to-batch variability in the HaloLigand-conjugated primer is a real and consequential risk

---

### Step B3 — Cell-Free Translation and Cis HaloTag Self-Assembly
🔴 **High variability**

**Description**

- RNA:cDNA hybrid pool added to E. coli cell-free translation system
- Release factors excluded from the reaction to stall ribosomes at stop codons — improves cis-coupling efficiency
- Translation order: HaloTag (N-terminal) → FLAG tag → ORF protein
- As nascent HaloTag domain folds, it forms an irreversible covalent bond with the HaloLigand on the nearby UCI cDNA — linking barcode to protein in cis
- ~50% of protein-UCI conjugates form in cis; ~50% form in trans (barcode from one molecule coupling to HaloTag of a nearby different molecule)
- 50% cis efficiency is sufficient for assay performance — trans events contribute to characterisable background estimated by mock IP controls

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Anti-FLAG western blot to confirm translation of HaloTag-FLAG-ORF fusion protein — confirmed in Credle & Larman 2022
- ✓ Test IP of a known positive antigen (e.g. TRIM21, NT5C1A) with validated positive serum — confirmed in Credle & Larman 2022
- ◇ Estimate cis coupling efficiency by HaloLigand bead pull-down followed by qPCR of UCI region
- ◇ Negative control: translation without HaloLigand-conjugated primer (should produce protein but no protein-UCI conjugate)

**Variability Introduced**

- Cis vs trans coupling ratio is inherently stochastic and varies by ORF size — larger proteins are released from ribosome before HaloTag matures, favouring trans coupling
- 50% cis efficiency is an average; actual rate varies per ORF — fundamental source of UCI-level efficiency variation
- This step is the primary statistical rationale for the proposed probe-aggregation model: UCI-level efficiency must be estimated, not assumed uniform
- Release factor exclusion improves cis rate but introduces ribosome stalling — a biological trade-off managed empirically

---

## Phase C: Immunoprecipitation

---

### Step C1 — Sample Preparation and Dilution
🟡 **Medium variability**

**Description**

- Patient or control serum/plasma diluted in IP buffer (typically 1:100 to 1:500)
- Processed in 96-well plate format
- Column 12 reserved for internal controls: pooled serum controls (same lot across all plates) and PBS mock IP controls (beads only, no serum)
- Each sample individually compared against the full set of mock IP controls in statistical analysis

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Column 12 control layout (serum controls + mock IPs) — confirmed in Infinity Bio VirSIGHT report
- ✓ Consistent dilution factor across all samples — confirmed standard practice
- ◇ Confirm sample identity and volume
- ◇ Flag samples with haemolysis or lipaemia (affects IgG recovery)

**Variability Introduced**

- Sample quality (haemolysis, freeze-thaw history) varies across biobank specimens
- Dilution factor affects the competition landscape — higher dilution reduces sensitivity but improves specificity
- Column 12 control design is the most explicit QC structure documented in the Infinity Bio operational protocol

---

### Step C2 — Incubation of Serum with MIPSA Library
🟡 **Medium variability**

**Description**

- Diluted serum mixed with MIPSA protein-barcode library and incubated at 4°C with rotation for 16–18 hours
- Serum antibodies bind to cognate antigens in solution
- Solution-phase binding kinetics more closely approximate native immunoassay conditions than phage display
- Conformational epitopes accessible — proteins are soluble and unconstrained by phage capsid geometry

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Positive control serum with known reactivity included on each plate — confirmed standard practice
- ✓ Mock IP (PBS) controls in column 12 — confirmed in VirSIGHT report
- ◇ Consistent library input across samples (normalised by protein concentration)
- ◇ Temperature and rotation speed logged for each run

**Variability Introduced**

- Total IgG varies between individuals — affects competition for library members
- Temperature fluctuations and rotation inconsistencies affect binding kinetics
- 16–18 hour window introduces time-of-day variability if plates not processed simultaneously

---

### Step C3 — Immunoprecipitation with Protein A/G Magnetic Beads
🔴 **High variability**

**Description**

- Protein A/G magnetic beads added to capture IgG–antigen complexes
- Beads separated magnetically and washed 3–5 times
- Antibody-bound MIPSA library members (protein + covalently linked UCI cDNA barcode) retained on beads
- Structurally equivalent to PhIP-Seq C3, but targeting soluble protein-DNA conjugates rather than intact phage particles

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Mock IP control (PBS) run in parallel — confirmed in VirSIGHT report; primary background reference for all statistical comparisons
- ✓ Positive control antigen recovery confirmed — confirmed standard practice
- ◇ Wash number and volume consistent across all samples
- ◇ Bead lot inter-lot validation before use in new library experiments

**Variability Introduced**

- Same bead-capture variability as PhIP-Seq C3
- Additional risk: MIPSA proteins are soluble — incomplete washing releases more background than from intact phage particles
- Trans-coupled barcode-protein pairs (from B3) contribute to non-specific background not distinguishable from true signal at the individual library member level
- Bead lot variation is a batch-level risk

---

## Phase D: Sequencing Library Preparation and NGS

---

### Step D1 — PCR Amplification of UCI Barcodes
🟡 **Medium variability**

**Description**

- After washing, beads resuspended and UCI cDNA barcodes amplified by PCR
- Universal primers flanking UCI region used, with Illumina adapters and sample-specific indices added
- UCIs are short (~50 bp) — PCR is efficient and requires fewer cycles than for PhIP-Seq inserts
- Each sample generates one indexed sequencing library

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Gel electrophoresis to confirm PCR product at expected size — confirmed standard practice
- ✓ Quantify libraries (Qubit or qPCR) — confirmed standard practice
- ◇ Check for primer dimer contamination
- ◇ Confirm index diversity across multiplexed samples

**Variability Introduced**

- PCR cycle number affects representation — more cycles introduce greater amplification bias
- Jackpot effects possible if input barcode counts are very low
- Short UCI amplicons are less susceptible to length bias than PhIP-Seq inserts

---

### Step D2 — Next-Generation Sequencing
🟢 **Low variability**

**Description**

- Multiplexed libraries pooled and sequenced on Illumina (NextSeq or HiSeq)
- Target: 1–3 million reads per sample
- Single-end reads standard — UCIs are short fixed-length sequences, paired-end adds no information
- Higher alignment rates than PhIP-Seq due to short, structured barcode targets

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Per-sample aligned read count (target: >500,000; low counts trigger repeat) — confirmed in VirSIGHT report
- ✓ Sequencing quality scores (Q30 threshold) — standard Illumina QC
- ✓ Alignment rate to validated UCI dictionary (target: >90%) — confirmed in VirSIGHT report
- ✓ Per-sample Pearson correlation with serum controls (target: ≥0.90 among column 12 controls) — confirmed in VirSIGHT report

**Variability Introduced**

- NGS is the most reproducible step in the pipeline
- Main risk: uneven sample pooling before sequencing run
- Run-to-run variability is low given standardised Illumina chemistry

---

## Phase E: Data Analysis

---

### Step E1 — Barcode-to-ORF Mapping and Count Matrix Generation
🟢 **Low variability**

**Description**

- Raw reads aligned using Bowtie2 to a validated dictionary of mono-associated barcode-ORF pairs
- Only UCIs confirmed to associate with a single ORF (by prior sequencing of unselected library) are retained
- Count matrix generated: rows = UCI-ORF pairs, columns = samples, values = read counts
- Multi-UCI structure per ORF is explicit in the matrix — each ORF has ~10 rows (one per UCI)

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ Alignment rate to validated UCI dictionary (target: >90%) — confirmed in VirSIGHT report
- ✓ Per-sample read depth — confirmed in VirSIGHT report
- ✓ Pearson correlation heatmap of serum controls across plates (target: ≥0.90) — confirmed in VirSIGHT report
- ◇ Flag samples with anomalously low read counts or low inter-control correlation
- ◇ PCA — mock IPs must cluster separately from serum samples

**Variability Introduced**

- Alignment is a deterministic computational step — minimal variability for fixed aligner parameters
- Validated UCI dictionary must be version-controlled and matched to the specific library lot used
- UCI dictionary validation is a one-time upstream step with its own sequencing QC

---

### Step E2 — Hit Calling with edgeR
🟡 **Medium variability**

**Description**

- Each sample compared against the full set of mock IP controls using edgeR (negative binomial model)
- Fold-over-background (FOB) calculated per UCI per sample
- Hits defined at FDR-adjusted p-value < 0.05
- Secondary confirmation rule applied: antigen called reactive if multiple UCIs targeting same ORF are independently significant
- Current pipeline treats each UCI as an independent observation — no formal probe-aggregation model is applied

**Potential QC Procedures**

- ✓ FOB distribution check (approximately log-normal with heavy right tail) — confirmed standard practice
- ✓ Positive control reactivity confirmed at expected FOB — confirmed in VirSIGHT report
- ✓ Mock IP Pearson correlation ≥ 0.90 among column 12 controls — confirmed in VirSIGHT report
- ◇ Mock IPs cluster separately from serum samples in PCA

**Variability Introduced**

- Current per-UCI, per-test approach does not model UCI-level efficiency — variation from B3 (cis vs trans coupling) is absorbed into noise rather than explicitly estimated
- Multi-UCI confirmation rule is a conservative heuristic — reduces false positives at cost of sensitivity for antigens with low cis-coupling efficiency or few UCIs
- FDR-based thresholds carry all the limitations of p-value-derived inference at scale
- Primary analytical limitation motivating the proposed RMA-like probe-aggregation model

---

# Comparative Summary: PhIP-Seq vs MIPSA

| Dimension | PhIP-Seq | MIPSA | Key Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Library format** | Peptide tiles on phage | Full-length proteins OR peptide tiles, soluble | MIPSA enables conformational epitope detection |
| **Barcode linkage** | Phage genome IS the barcode | Covalent HaloTag–HaloLigand bond | MIPSA barcoding is chemical, not biological |
| **Highest variability step** | Phage panning (C2/C3) | RT + self-assembly (B2/B3) | Different mechanistic bottlenecks |
| **Background control** | Mock IP (PBS panning) | Mock IP (PBS, column 12) | Structurally equivalent |
| **Hit calling** | Per-tile edgeR, BEER, or Z-score | Per-UCI edgeR + multi-UCI confirmation | MIPSA has explicit designed-in redundancy |
| **Conformational epitopes** | No | Yes (full-length library) | Fundamental biological difference |
| **Protocol maturity** | High (v4, video protocol, widely replicated) | Medium (v3, Infinity Bio operational, less openly documented) | PhIP-Seq has more community validation |

---

*Primary sources: Larman et al. (2011); Mohan & Larman et al. (2018); Credle & Larman et al. (2022); Larman lab bioRxiv (2021); Infinity Bio VirSIGHT Report (2024); Frontiers in Bioinformatics review (2024).*
